reader_question: Do rents run higher where renters earn more, and where does rent take the largest share of renters’ income?
title: Higher rents went with higher renter incomes across the states in 2025, and rent took the largest share of renters’ income in Florida, 35.5 percent.
measure_line: Median gross rent a month against renter households’ median income a year, 2025, 50 states and DC; each dot is a state.
reading_guide: States to the right have renters with higher incomes, and states higher up have higher rents. States above the cloud pay more rent for their income.
notes: This shows the two move together; it does not show one causes the other.

Rent as a percent of income is the Census Bureau’s own measure: the median, across renter households paying cash rent, of each one’s rent over its income. Florida’s 35.5 percent (margin 0.5) passes the next figures, California’s 32.9 (0.3) and Hawaii’s 32.8 (1.2), by more than their margins. Margins of error are at 90 percent confidence.
North Dakota has the smallest figure, 23.8 percent (margin 1.2); Wyoming’s 25.5 (2.0) sits within its margin, so the survey cannot order the two.
alt: A scatter plot of 50 states and DC: median gross rent against renter households’ median income in 2025. The dots climb from lower left to upper right, from West Virginia’s $921 rent to California’s $2,160. Florida, named in dark ink, sits above the cloud: its rent takes 35.5 percent of renters’ income, the largest share.
